### Detailed Explanation of B-Tree Insertion, Splitting, and Rebalancing

A B-tree is a self-balancing tree data structure that maintains sorted data and allows searches, sequential access, insertions, and deletions in logarithmic time. Unlike binary search trees, B-trees are designed to work well with disk-based storage systems because they keep data in sorted order and allow for efficient range queries. The key characteristic of a B-tree of order $m$ is that every node has at most $m$ children and at least $\lceil m/2 \rceil$ children (except for the root, which can have as few as 2 children if it is not a leaf). Consequently, every internal node (except the root) contains between $\lceil m/2 \rceil - 1$ and $m - 1$ keys. All leaves appear at the same level, ensuring the tree remains balanced.

The insertion process in a B-tree is distinct from that of a binary search tree because it is performed "bottom-up" in terms of structural changes, even though the search for the insertion point is top-down.
